passage:
Dear Trisha,

You would have loved last Saturday. I was walking back from the library when a wedding baraat came down our street: a white horse and drummers, cousins dancing so hard their turbans slipped, and a small girl on someone's shoulders throwing petals. I stopped at the kerb. To me it looked like pure joy, but the woman beside me said quietly that the groom's grandmother had died last year and this was the first celebration since. So for her the noise also held a little missing. I don't know the family, so I just clapped when they passed and stayed out of the way. I'm still thinking about how one procession can say two things.

Write soon.
Ojas

qa.q: What did the small girl throw as the baraat passed?
qa.a: She threw petals from someone's shoulders.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling as Ojas watched the baraat, and how did the woman's remark complicate it?
qa.a: To Ojas it looked like pure joy, and the woman added that it was the first celebration since the groom's grandmother died, so it also held a little missing.

qa.q: How could Ojas respectfully learn more about what a procession means?
qa.a: Ojas could observe from the side, stay out of the way, and ask someone from the family or community what it means to them.

qa.q: How might the groom's family feel about the procession compared with a passer-by?
qa.a: The family may feel joy and loss together, while a passer-by like Ojas may see only the celebration.

grounding: Ojas reads a wedding procession as joy and learns from a bystander that it also carries loss.

passage: So I'm Saurabh, and I was on exchange in Edinburgh when I first stood on the pavement watching a graduation march. Hundreds of students in black gowns and coloured hoods walked slowly behind a piper, and I assumed it was pure celebration. Then my flatmate Chetan, who'd graduated the year before, said, "Look at their faces. Some are happy and some are relieved, and the ones near the back are thinking about who couldn't be here." I hadn't thought of that. I asked him what the hoods meant and he said each colour showed a subject. I kept quiet as they passed. I realised the walk felt solemn to them, not just festive, and I'd only have known by asking.

qa.q: Which city was Saurabh in on exchange?
qa.a: Saurabh was on exchange in Edinburgh.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling about the march at first, and how did Chetan's remark change that view?
qa.a: Saurabh assumed it was pure celebration, and Chetan added that some students look happy, some relieved, and some are thinking about people who couldn't be there.

qa.q: What could Saurabh do to understand this ceremony better?
qa.a: Saurabh could ask people who took part what the march and hoods mean to them and observe respectfully.

qa.q: How might a graduate see the slow walk behind the piper?
qa.a: It may feel solemn and meaningful to them, marking an end and a beginning, more than just a party.

grounding: Saurabh reads a graduation march as celebration and learns from a friend that it carries solemn meanings too.

passage: I'm Parveen, and I was walking with Pankaj through the old town in Kochi when we heard drums and a brass band coming round the corner. Pankaj, just arrived from Delhi, grinned and pulled out his phone. "A wedding! Let's film the baraat!" Then the procession came into view. Men in white walked slowly behind a flower-covered bier. The band played, but the faces were still and wet-eyed. Pankaj lowered his phone, his grin fading. He looked at me, confused. I wasn't sure either; I'd grown up in Kerala but never in this community. We stepped back against a shop wall. The shopkeeper, an old man, said quietly, "An old teacher. Ninety-two. The band is for a full life." Pankaj nodded and put his phone away. He stood with his hands folded until the procession passed. I don't know exactly what he felt, but he was silent for the next ten minutes.

qa.q: How old was the teacher who had died?
qa.a: Ninety-two.

qa.q: What might Pankaj have been feeling as the procession came into view?
qa.a: His fading grin and lowered phone suggest he felt confused and embarrassed, realising it was a funeral, not a wedding.

qa.q: What did Pankaj and Parveen do that showed respect?
qa.a: They stepped back, Pankaj put his phone away and folded his hands, and they asked the shopkeeper instead of guessing.

qa.q: How did the shopkeeper explain the band?
qa.a: He said the band was for a full life, since the old teacher was ninety-two.

grounding: Shows through an observer a young adult reading a procession as a wedding, then learning it was a funeral, and watching respectfully and asking.

passage:
Day one. On Varun's first week in Lucknow for his internship, he heard slow drumming and saw people in black walking through the old city at night, some beating their chests. He assumed it was a festival and asked a passer-by, "Which celebration is this?" The man looked at him sadly and walked on. Varun's face burned.
Day two. He asked Vidya, his colleague who had grown up in the old city. "It's Muharram," she said gently. "For many Shia families it's a time of mourning, remembering a great loss in their history. It isn't a celebration." Varun felt awful about his question.
Day four. Vidya took him to watch the procession from her aunt's balcony. Varun stayed quiet, watching the black flags and the faces. When a young man looked up, Varun bowed his head slightly. Vidya's aunt offered him sherbet. "You came to understand," she said. "That's respect."

qa.q: Where did Vidya take Varun to watch the procession?
qa.a: From her aunt's balcony.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling after the passer-by walked away?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, his face burning, realising his question may have hurt someone in mourning.

qa.q: What did Varun do that helped him understand?
qa.a: He asked Vidya, who knew the tradition, and then watched quietly and respectfully from the balcony.

qa.q: How did Vidya's aunt see Varun's presence at the procession?
qa.a: She saw it as respect, because he came to understand rather than to watch for fun.

grounding: Shows a young adult misreading a mourning procession as celebration and learning to observe respectfully and ask.

passage: Jagdish, since you're going to Scotland for your master's, let your Harsha uncle tell you a story. When I was twenty-one, I went to Edinburgh on a short exchange. On my first Saturday I heard bagpipes, slow and wailing, and saw a long line of people in black gowns walking two by two up the hill. I thought someone important had died. I took off my cap, stood very still by the road and bowed my head. A girl in a gown broke line, laughed and handed me a flyer. "It's graduation! We're celebrating!" I felt so foolish. For us, that slow wailing music sounds like mourning. For them, it was pride. That evening I asked my hostel warden to explain the robes, the colours and the march. He talked for an hour, delighted that I asked. Watch first, beta. Then ask. The music doesn't always mean what it means at home.

qa.q: What did the girl hand young Harsha?
qa.a: A flyer.

qa.q: How did young Harsha feel when the girl said it was graduation?
qa.a: He felt foolish and embarrassed, having taken the slow bagpipes and black gowns as signs of mourning.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Harsha understand the march?
qa.a: That evening he asked his hostel warden to explain the robes, colours and march, instead of just guessing.

qa.q: How did the girl in the gown see Harsha's bowed head?
qa.a: She found it funny, laughing and handing him a flyer to explain it was a celebration.

grounding: Shows a young adult misreading a graduation march as a funeral and learning that tradition sets the meaning, so observing and asking helps.

passage: The auto was stuck on the Lucknow ring road in a drizzle, and Pema, three weeks into her college year, pressed her face to the plastic window. First came a crowd dancing behind a white horse, dhol thundering, a man tossing coins into the air. "Wedding," Lalit said, grinning. "The groom's side, the baraat. They'll dance all the way to the venue." Pema laughed and filmed a few seconds. Twenty minutes later a second procession passed on foot, slower: men in white carrying a bamboo bier covered in marigolds, chanting in low voices. Pema started to raise her phone again, then stopped. Their faces were different. "Is this also a celebration?" she whispered. "No," Lalit said quietly. "A funeral. They're going to the ghat." Pema lowered the phone and bowed her head until they had passed. "In Gangtok our funeral processions have monks and prayer flags," she said. "I wouldn't have known this one." "That's why you asked," Lalit said.

qa.q: What were the men in the second procession carrying?
qa.a: A bamboo bier covered in marigolds.

qa.q: Why did Pema stop raising her phone at the second procession?
qa.a: Pema felt unsure and cautious, sensing from the slow pace, white clothes, low chanting and faces that this was different, so she chose respect over filming.

qa.q: What did Pema do that an outsider should do?
qa.a: Watch respectfully, lower the phone, and quietly ask what the procession meant.

qa.q: How might the mourners have felt if Pema had filmed them?
qa.a: Probably intruded upon at a moment of grief.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult outsider reading a baraat as joy and a funeral procession as loss, observing respectfully and asking rather than guessing.
